title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 10–11 (Night 224, continuing nights-223), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 224 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The treasurer, saved from the lion by al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, embraces them and refuses to do the deed their father ordered: he takes their clothes, dresses them in his own, fills two flasks with the lion's blood and sends them off into God's wide earth. Back at court, King Qamar al-Zamān takes the treasurer's shaken face for the mark of the killing and rejoices; he receives the bundles and the blood, and hears the princes' last message — that he is forgiven their blood — and two lines of verse on the guile of women. The king bows his head, understands that his sons were killed unjustly, and weeps over their clothes, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-fourth night,
sentences.n: As at every night's opening: the unit, al-rābiʿatu, comes before the tens and is joined to them by wa-, and both stand in the nominative with al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْخَازِنْدَارَ قَالَ لِلْأَمْجَدِ وَالْأَسْعَدِ بِرُوحِي أَفْدِيكُمَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-khāzindāra qāla li-al-Amjadi wa-al-Asʿadi bi-rūḥī afdīkumā
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-treasurer said to-al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad: With-my-soul I-ransom-you-two.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the treasurer said to al-Amjad and al-Asʿad: I would give my own life for yours.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the last words of the night before. As there, the print runs al-saʿīdu and anna together as one word, السعيدان; it is kept as set and read as the two words al-saʿīdu anna, “fortunate, that”; anna takes its noun, al-khāzindāra, in the accusative. li-al-Amjadi, “to al-Amjad”: li- marks the ones spoken to. bi-rūḥī afdīkumā, “with my soul I ransom you”: bi- marks what is given in exchange, and the phrase is set first for weight.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَهَضَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ وَاعْتَنَقَهُمَا وَسَأَلَهُمَا عَنْ سَبَبِ فَكِّ وِثَاقِهِمَا وَقُدُومِهِمَا
sentences.tr: thumma nahaḍa min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi wa-iʿtanaqahumā wa-saʾalahumā ʿan sababi fakki withāqihimā wa-qudūmihimā
sentences.l: Then he-rose from his-time and-his-hour, and-embraced-them-two and-asked-them-two about (the) cause (of the) undoing (of) their-two-bond and-their-two-coming.
sentences.i: Then he rose that very moment and embraced them, and asked them how their bonds had come to be undone and what had brought them there.
sentences.n: min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from his time and his hour”, the storyteller's phrase for “at once”. iʿtanaqa, Form VIII of ʿ-n-q, “to embrace”, here with a direct object. saʾala ʿan, “to ask about”: ʿan marks the matter asked about; the print writes وسالهما without its hamza. fakk, verbal noun of fakka, “to undo, unfasten”; its shadda, فكّ, is printed. withāq (also wathāq), “bond, cord”. qudūm, “coming, arrival”.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرَاهُ أَنَّهُمَا عَطِشَا وَانْحَلَّ الْوِثَاقُ مِنْ أَحَدِهِمَا فَفَكَّ الْآخَرَ بِسَبَبِ خُلُوصِ نِيَّتِهِمَا ثُمَّ أَنَّهُمَا اقْتَصَّا الْأَثَرَ حَتَّى وَصَلَا إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbarāhu annahumā ʿaṭishā wa-inḥalla al-withāqu min aḥadihimā fa-fakka al-ākhara bi-sababi khulūṣi niyyatihimā thumma annahumā iqtaṣṣā al-athara ḥattā waṣalā ilayhi
sentences.l: So-they-two-told-him that-they-two thirsted, and-came-loose the-bond from one-of-them-two, so-he-undid the-other, by-reason-of (the) purity (of) their-two-intention; then that-they-two followed the-track until they-two-reached him.
sentences.i: They told him that they had grown thirsty, and that the bond of one of them had come loose, so that he set the other free, thanks to the purity of their intentions; and that they had then followed the tracks until they reached him.
sentences.n: akhbara, Form IV of kh-b-r, “to tell”, takes the one told as its object, -hu, and the news as an anna clause. ʿaṭishā, “they two grew thirsty”, dual of ʿaṭisha. inḥalla, Form VII of ḥ-l-l, “to come undone”. fa-fakka al-ākhara, “and he undid the other”: the one who had worked loose frees his brother, as in the night before. bi-sababi, “by reason of”: bi- of cause. khulūṣ niyyatihimā, “the purity of their intention”: their innocence is named as what loosed the cord. thumma annahumā carries the report on under akhbarāhu, “and then (they told him) that they”. iqtaṣṣa al-athara, Form VIII of q-ṣ-ṣ, “to follow the track”. The shaddas of وانحلّ, ففكّ, نيّتهما and اقتصّا and the آ of الآخر are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامَهُمَا شَكَرَهُمَا عَلَى فِعْلِهِمَا وَخَرَجَ مَعَهُمَا إِلَى ظَاهِرِ الْغَابَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kalāmahumā shakarahumā ʿalā fiʿlihimā wa-kharaja maʿahumā ilā ẓāhiri al-ghābati
sentences.l: And-when he-heard their-two-speech, he-thanked-them-two for their-two-deed, and-went-out with-them-two to (the) outside (of) the-wood.
sentences.i: When he heard what they said, he thanked them for what they had done and went out with them to the edge of the wood.
sentences.n: shakara ʿalā, “to thank for”: ʿalā marks what one is thanked for. fiʿl, “deed, act”. ẓāhir, “outside, outer part”: ẓāhir al-ghābati is the open ground just beyond the trees.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا صَارُوا فِي ظَاهِرِ الْغَابَةِ قَالَا لَهُ يَا عَمِّ افْعَلْ مَا أَمَرَكَ بِهِ أَبُونَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṣārū fī ẓāhiri al-ghābati qālā lahu yā ʿammi ifʿal mā amaraka bihi abūnā
sentences.l: And-when they-came-to-be in (the) outside (of) the-wood, they-two-said to-him: O uncle, do what commanded-you with-it our-father.
sentences.i: When they were out of the wood, they said to him: Uncle, do what our father commanded you.
sentences.n: ṣārū, “they came to be”, plural, for the three of them; qālā, dual, for the two brothers. yā ʿammi, “O uncle”: ʿamm, “father's brother”, is a respectful address to an older man. amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes the thing commanded with bi-, and bihi, “with it”, takes up mā, “what”. abūnā, “our father”, nominative as the subject of amara.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ حَاشَى لِلّٰهِ أَنْ أَقْرَبَكُمَا بِضَرَرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ḥāshā li-Allāhi an aqrabakumā bi-ḍararin
sentences.l: So-he-said: Far-be-it, for-God, that I-come-near-you-two with-harm!
sentences.i: He said: God forbid that I should come near you to do you harm!
sentences.n: ḥāshā li-Allāhi, “God forbid”, literally “far be it, for God's sake”: li- marks God, before whom the thing is disowned. The print spells ḥāshā with yāʾ, حاشى, where the usual spelling ends in alif, حاشا; it is kept as printed. The kasra of لِله is printed. an aqrabakumā, “that I should come near you”: qariba, “to approach”, takes its object directly, and an puts it in the subjunctive. bi-ḍararin, “with harm”: bi- marks what he would bring.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنِ اعْلَمَا أَنِّي أُرِيدُأَنْ أَنْزِعَ ثِيَابَكُمَا وَأُلْبِسَكُمَا ثِيَابِي وَأَمْلَأَ قَنَانِيتَيْنِ مِنْ دَمِ الْأَسَدِ ثُمَّ أَرُوحَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ وَأَقُولَ لَهُ إِنِّي قَتَلْتُهُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-lākini iʿlamā annī urīdu an anziʿa thiyābakumā wa-ulbisakumā thiyābī wa-amlaʾa qanānītayni min dami al-asadi thumma arūḥa ilā al-maliki wa-aqūla lahu innī qataltuhumā
sentences.l: But know-you-two that-I want that I-strip-off your-two-clothes and-I-clothe-you-two (in) my-clothes, and-I-fill two-flasks from (the) blood (of) the-lion; then I-go to the-king and-I-say to-him: Indeed-I killed-them-two.
sentences.i: But know that I mean to take off your clothes and dress you in mine, and fill two flasks with the lion's blood; then I will go to the king and tell him that I have killed you.
sentences.n: The print runs urīdu and an together as one word, اريدان; it is kept as set and read as the two words urīdu an, “I want to”. iʿlamā, dual imperative of ʿalima, “know”; lākin takes a kasra before the joined alif. nazaʿa, “to strip off”; albasa, Form IV of l-b-s, “to clothe”, takes two objects, the person and the garment: ulbisakumā thiyābī, “clothe you in my clothes”. All the verbs after an are subjunctive: anziʿa, ulbisa, amlaʾa, arūḥa, aqūla. qanānītayni, “two flasks”, is a dual built on qanānī, the plural of qinnīna, “flask, bottle”, as though from a singular qanānīya; the form is unusual and its vowelling here is a guess, but the print has it three times in this night. malaʾa min, “to fill with”: min marks what fills. rāḥa, “to go”, a verb of the spoken language. After qāla the words take inna: innī qataltuhumā, “I have killed them”, the report as he will speak it. The أ of واملأ is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا أَنْتُمَا فَسِيحَا فِى الْبِلَادِ وَأَرْضُ اللّٰهِ وَاسِعَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā antumā fa-sīḥā fī al-bilādi wa-arḍu Allāhi wāsiʿatun
sentences.l: And-as-for you-two, then-roam-you-two in the-lands, and-(the)-earth (of) God (is) wide.
sentences.i: As for you, go and wander through the lands; God's earth is wide.
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-, “and as for … (then)”: ammā is answered by fa-. sīḥā, dual imperative of sāḥa, yasīḥu, “to roam the land”, a hollow verb. wa-arḍu Allāhi wāsiʿatun, “and God's earth is wide”, a proverbial phrase that echoes the Qurʾān (4:97, 39:10). The print spells fī with ى, فى.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمَا يَاسَيِّدَايَ أَنَّ فِرَاقَكُمَا يَعِزُّ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlamā yā sayyidāya anna firāqakumā yaʿizzu ʿalayya
sentences.l: And-know-you-two, O my-two-masters, that parting-(from)-you-two is-hard upon-me.
sentences.i: And know, my lords, that it grieves me to part from you.
sentences.n: The print runs yā and sayyidāya together, ياسيداي; it is kept as set. yā sayyidāya, “O my two masters”: the dual keeps its nominative form before the suffix, as in the night before. firāq, “parting”, verbal noun of Form III fāraqa; the suffix -kumā names the ones parted from. ʿazza ʿalā, “to be hard on, grieve”: ʿalā marks the one it weighs on. The shaddas of يعزّ and عليّ are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى كُلٌّ مِنَ الْخَازِنْدَارِ وَالْغُلَامَيْنِ وَقَدْ قَلَعَا ثِيَابَهُمَا وَأَلْبَسَهُمَا ثِيَابَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma bakā kullun mina al-khāzindāri wa-al-ghulāmayni wa-qad qalaʿā thiyābahumā wa-albasahumā thiyābahu
sentences.l: Then wept each of the-treasurer and-the-two-youths; and-they-two-had pulled-off their-two-clothes, and-he-clothed-them-two (in) his-clothes.
sentences.i: Then the treasurer and the two youths all wept; the boys took off their clothes, and he dressed them in his own.
sentences.n: kullun min, “each of”: kull standing without a following noun takes tanwīn, and min names the group. ghulām, “youth, lad”, here in the dual. wa-qad qalaʿā, “and they had taken off”: qalaʿa, “to pull out, uproot”, is the spoken language's word for taking off clothes, where Classical says khalaʿa. albasa again takes two objects, -humā and thiyābahu.

sentences.t: وَرَاحَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ وَقَدْ أَخَذَ ذٰلِكَ وَرَبَطَ قُمَاشَ كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا فِي بُقْجَةٍ مَعَهُ وَمَلَأَ الْقَنَانِيتَيْنِ مِنْ دَمِ الْأَسَدِ وَجَعَلَ الْبُقْجَتَيْنِ قُدَّامَهُ عَلَى ظَهْرِ الْجَوَادِ
sentences.tr: wa-rāḥa ilā al-maliki wa-qad akhadha dhālika wa-rabaṭa qumāsha kulli wāḥidin minhumā fī buqjatin maʿahu wa-malaʾa al-qanānītayni min dami al-asadi wa-jaʿala al-buqjatayni quddāmahu ʿalā ẓahri al-jawādi
sentences.l: And-he-went to the-king, and-he-had taken that: and-he-tied (the) stuff (of) each one of-them-two in a-bundle with-him, and-filled the-two-flasks from (the) blood (of) the-lion, and-put the-two-bundles in-front-of-him on (the) back (of) the-steed.
sentences.i: And he went off to the king, having taken all this with him: he had tied up the clothes of each of them in a bundle to carry, and filled the two flasks with the lion's blood, and he set the two bundles before him on the horse's back.
sentences.n: The storyteller names the journey first, wa-rāḥa ilā al-maliki, and then goes back over what was taken: wa-qad akhadha dhālika, “having taken that”, and the verbs after it say what “that” was. qumāsh, “cloth, stuff”, here the clothes. buqja, “a bundle tied up in a wrapping-cloth”, a loanword from Turkish (bohça). quddāma, “in front of”, a word of the spoken language; its shadda, قدّامه, is printed. jawād, “steed, fine horse”. The أ of وملأ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ وَدَّعَهُمَا وَسَارَ مُتَوَجِّهًا إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ سَائِرًا حَتَّى دَخَلَ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma waddaʿahumā wa-sāra mutawajjihan ilā al-madīnati wa-lam yazal sāʾiran ḥattā dakhala ʿalā al-maliki wa-qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: Then he-bade-farewell-to-them-two and-travelled heading to the-city, and-not he-ceased travelling until he-entered upon the-king and-kissed the-ground between his-two-hands.
sentences.i: Then he bade them farewell and set off for the city, and he rode on until he came in to the king and kissed the ground before him.
sentences.n: waddaʿa, Form II of w-d-ʿ, “to bid farewell to”. mutawajjihan, Form V participle of w-j-h, “heading for”, an accusative of state. lam yazal sāʾiran, “he did not cease going”: lam yazal with a participle, “kept on”. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to” a person: ʿalā marks the one visited. qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhi, “kissed the ground between his hands”, the courtly prostration before a king. The shaddas of ودّعهما, متوجّها and وقبّل and the ئ of سائرا are printed.

sentences.t: فَرَآهُ الْمَلِكُ مُتَغَيِّرَ الْوَجْهِ وَذٰلِكَ مِمَّا جَرَى لَهُ مِنَ الْأَسَدِ فَظَنَّ أَنَّ ذٰلِكَ مِنْ قَتْلِ أَوْلَادِهِ فَفَرِحَ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾāhu al-maliku mutaghayyira al-wajhi wa-dhālika mimmā jarā lahu mina al-asadi fa-ẓanna anna dhālika min qatli awlādihi fa-fariḥa
sentences.l: And-saw-him the-king changed (of) the-face — and-that (was) from-what happened to-him from the-lion — so-he-thought that that (was) from (the) killing (of) his-children, and-he-rejoiced.
sentences.i: The king saw that his face was changed — which came of what had befallen him with the lion — and, thinking it came of killing his sons, he was glad.
sentences.n: The print has اولادة, a misprint for اولاده, corrected here. mutaghayyira al-wajhi, “changed of face”, an accusative of state in construct with a definite noun, like ʿaẓīmu al-khaṭari the night before. mimmā, min with mā, “from what”: min gives the cause, as again in min qatli awlādihi, “from killing his sons”. jarā li-, “to happen to”. awlād, plural of walad, “child, son”, used here of the two. The آ of فرآه and the shaddas of متغيّر and فظنّ are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ هَلْ قَضَيْتَ الشُّغْلَ قَالَ نَعَمْ يَا مَوْلَانَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu hal qaḍayta al-shughla qāla naʿam yā mawlānā
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Have you-accomplished the-work? He-said: Yes, O our-master.
sentences.i: He said to him: Have you done the job? He said: Yes, my lord.
sentences.n: hal, the particle of a yes-or-no question. qaḍā, “to settle, carry through”; the fatḥa on the tāʾ of قضيتَ is printed. shughl, “work, business”, the everyday word for a task. yā mawlānā, “O our master”, the usual address to a king.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَاوَلَهُ الْبُقْجَتَيْنِ اللَّتَيْنِ فِيهِمَا الثِّيَابُ وَالْقَنَانِيتَيْنِ الْمُمْتَلِئَتَيْنِ بِالدَّمِ
sentences.tr: thumma nāwalahu al-buqjatayni allatayni fīhimā al-thiyābu wa-al-qanānītayni al-mumtaliʾatayni bi-al-dami
sentences.l: Then he-handed-him the-two-bundles which in-them-two (are) the-clothes, and-the-two-flasks the-two-filled with-the-blood.
sentences.i: Then he handed him the two bundles with the clothes in them, and the two flasks full of blood.
sentences.n: nāwala, Form III of n-w-l, “to hand over”, takes both the receiver, -hu, and the thing handed as objects. allatayni, the feminine dual relative in the oblique case, agrees with al-buqjatayni; fīhimā al-thiyābu, “in them (are) the clothes”, is its clause. al-mumtaliʾatayni, Form VIII participle of m-l-ʾ, “filled”; bi- marks what they are filled with. The ئ of الممتلئتين is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ مَا ذَا رَأَيْتَ مِنْهُمَا وَهَلْ أَوْصَيَاكَ بِشَيْءٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku mā dhā raʾayta minhumā wa-hal awṣayāka bi-shayʾin
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-king: What (is) it you-saw from-them-two? And-did they-two-charge-you with-a-thing?
sentences.i: The king said to him: What did you see of them? Did they charge you with any message?
sentences.n: mā dhā, “what (is it) that”, printed as two words. raʾā min, “to see from”, of how someone bore himself. awṣā, Form IV of w-ṣ-y, “to charge, enjoin, leave a last request with”, takes the thing enjoined with bi-. The أ of رأيت and the ء of بشيء are printed.

sentences.t: قَالَ وَجَدْتُهُمَا صَابِرَيْنِ مُحْتَسِبَيْنِ بِمَا نَزَلَ بِهِمَا
sentences.tr: qāla wajadtuhumā ṣābirayni muḥtasibayni bi-mā nazala bihimā
sentences.l: He-said: I-found-them-two patient, reckoning-(it-to-God) in-what came-down upon-them-two.
sentences.i: He said: I found them patient, bearing what had come upon them and looking to God for their reward.
sentences.n: ṣābirayni muḥtasibayni, “patient, resigned”, are read as duals, accusatives of state after wajada; the print's letters could equally be the plurals ṣābirīna muḥtasibīna, which the later language uses of two. iḥtasaba, Form VIII of ḥ-s-b, is to bear a loss reckoning it to God's account, in hope of His reward. bi-mā, “in what”: bi- marks the trial they bear. nazala bi-, “to come down upon, befall”: bi- marks the ones it falls on.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ قَالَ لِي إِنَّ أَبَانَا مَعْذُورٌ فَأَقْرِئْهُ مِنَّا السَّلَامَ وَقُلْ لَهُ أَنْتَ فِي حِلٍّ مِنْ قَتْلِنَا وَمِنْ دِمَائِنَا وَلٰكِنْ نُوصِيكَ أَنْ تُبَلِّغَهُ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ وَهُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad qāla lī inna abānā maʿdhūrun fa-aqriʾhu minnā al-salāma wa-qul lahu anta fī ḥillin min qatlinā wa-min dimāʾinā wa-lākin nūṣīka an tuballighahu hādhayni al-baytayni wa-humā
sentences.l: And-he-has said to-me: Indeed our-father (is) excused; so-convey-to-him from-us the-greeting, and-say to-him: You (are) in release from our-killing and-from our-blood. But we-charge-you that you-deliver-to-him these-two the-two-verses — and-they-two (are):
sentences.i: And they said to me: Our father is not to blame; give him our greeting, and tell him: You are quit of our killing and of our blood. But we charge you to bring him these two verses, which run:
sentences.n: wa-qad qāla lī, “and he said to me”: the verb is singular though both brothers speak, and what follows is in the first person plural, “our father … we charge you”; a singular verb for the pair is unexpected: either one brother speaks for both, or the print has dropped the alif of the dual, قالا, “they said”. The print's قال is kept. inna opens the quoted words after qāla; its shadda, انّ, is printed. maʿdhūr, “excused, not to blame”, passive participle of ʿadhara. aqraʾa, Form IV of q-r-ʾ, “to convey (a greeting) to”, takes two objects, the person, -hu, and al-salāma; the print writes its hamza on a yāʾ seat, فاقرئه. fī ḥillin min, “released from”: ḥill, “being quit of a claim”; the shadda of حلّ is printed. dimāʾ, plural of dam, “blood”, here the claim of blood-vengeance; the ئ of دمائنا is printed. awṣā, “to charge”, now with an and the subjunctive. ballagha, Form II of b-l-gh, “to deliver”, takes two objects, the person and the message; the shadda of تبلّغه is printed. hādhayni al-baytayni, “these two verses”, oblique dual. wa-humā, “and they are”, introduces the lines.

sentences.t:
اِنَّ النِّسَاءَ شَيَاطِينٌ خُلِقْنَ لَنَا * نَعُوذُ بِاللهِ مِنْ كَيْدِ الشَّيَاطِينِ
فَهُنَّ اِصْلُ الْبَلِيَّاتِ الَّتِيْ ظَهَرَتْ * بَيْنَ الْبَرِيَّةِ فِى الدُّنْيَا وَفِى الدِّينِ
sentences.tr:
inna al-nisāʾa shayāṭīnun khuliqna lanā * naʿūdhu bi-Allāhi min kaydi al-shayāṭīni
fa-hunna aṣlu al-baliyyāti allatī ẓaharat * bayna al-bariyyati fī al-dunyā wa-fī al-dīni
sentences.l:
Indeed the-women (are) devils created for-us; * we-take-refuge with-God from (the) guile (of) the-devils.
So-they (are the) root (of) the-calamities which appeared * among the-creation, in the-world and-in the-religion.
sentences.i:
Women are devils, created for us; * we seek refuge in God from the devils' guile.
They are the root of all the calamities that have appeared * among mankind, in this world and in religion.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre basīṭ, rhyming in -īni. shayāṭīnun takes tanwīn although the plural normally does not; the metre needs the long syllable, and the print sets it so. khuliqna, passive perfect, feminine plural, “they were created”. ʿādha bi-, “to take refuge with”: bi- marks the one in whom refuge is sought; naʿūdhu bi-Allāhi is the formula spoken against Satan, here turned on women. kayd, “guile, scheming”. The print sets a kasra under the alif of اِصْلُ; the word is aṣl, “root, origin”, which takes a fatḥa, and it is read aṣlu here, the printed mark kept. baliyyāt, plural of baliyya, “trial, calamity”. al-bariyya, “creation, mankind”. al-dunyā wa-al-dīn, “this world and religion”, the whole of a man's affairs. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare, اِنَّ and اِصْلُ, sets a sukūn on the last letter of الَّتِيْ, writes Allāh without its shadda, اللهِ, and spells fī with ى, فِى.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ مِنَ الْخَازِنْدَارِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ أَطْرَقَ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ مَلِيًّا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku mina al-khāzindāri hādhā al-kalāma aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi maliyyan
sentences.l: And-when heard the-king from the-treasurer this the-speech, he-bowed with-his-head to the-ground a-long-while.
sentences.i: When the king heard these words from the treasurer, he bowed his head to the ground for a long while.
sentences.n: aṭraqa, Form IV of ṭ-r-q, “to lower the eyes, bow the head in silence”; bi- marks the head as what is bowed. maliyyan, “for a long while”, an adverbial accusative; its shadda, مليّا, is printed, as is the أ of برأسه.

sentences.t: وَعَلِمَ أَنَّ كَلَامَ وَلَدَيْهِ هٰذَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّهُمَا قَدْ قُتُلَا ظُلْمًا
sentences.tr: wa-ʿalima anna kalāma waladayhi hādhā yadullu ʿalā annahumā qad qutilā ẓulman
sentences.l: And-he-knew that (the) speech (of) his-two-sons this points to that-they-two had been-killed (in) wrong.
sentences.i: And he knew that these words of his two sons showed they had been put to death unjustly.
sentences.n: waladayhi, “his two sons”, the dual of walad in construct, its nūn dropped before the suffix. dalla ʿalā, “to point to, show”: ʿalā marks what is shown; the shadda of يدلّ is printed. qad qutilā, “they have been killed”, passive perfect, dual. The print sets a ḍamma over the tāʾ, قتُلا, where the passive has a kasra; the mark seems to have slipped from the qāf. It is kept where it is printed, the qāf is given its ḍamma, and the word is read qutilā. ẓulman, “wrongfully”, an accusative of manner.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَفَكَّرَ فِي مَكْرِ النِّسَاءِ وَدَوَاهِيهِنَّ وَأَخَذَ الْبُقْجَتَيْنِ وَفَتَحَهُمَا وَصَارَ يُقَلِّبُ ثِيَابَ أَوْلَادِهِ وَيَبْكِي
sentences.tr: thumma tafakkara fī makri al-nisāʾi wa-dawāhīhinna wa-akhadha al-buqjatayni wa-fataḥahumā wa-ṣāra yuqallibu thiyāba awlādihi wa-yabkī
sentences.l: Then he-pondered on (the) cunning (of) the-women and-their-calamities; and-he-took the-two-bundles and-opened-them-two and-began he-turns-over (the) clothes (of) his-children and-he-weeps.
sentences.i: Then he thought on the cunning of women and their wiles, and he took the two bundles and opened them, and began to turn his sons' clothes over and over, weeping.
sentences.n: The print has اولادة, a misprint for اولاده, corrected here. tafakkara fī, Form V of f-k-r, “to reflect on”: fī marks the matter. makr, “cunning, deceit”. dawāhī, plural of dāhiya, “calamity”, and also “cunning trick”; with -hinna, “their”, of the women. ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to”. qallaba, Form II of q-l-b, “to turn over and over”. The shaddas of تفكّر and يقلّب and the ء of النساء are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
